compliances.complianceSummary: The CEO reviews the performance of other Directors (non-Corporate) and other senior managers at least annually.

The CEO and the Director Corporate Services, ensures there is the highest level of Corporate Services available. There are Board approved policies and procedures for the following;
a.)	Assets recording, management and reporting
b.)	Complaints handling
c.)	Corporate risks management and reporting
d.)	Delegations of Authority
e.)	Discipline and Disciplinary Process
f.)	Diversity, Gender and Social Obligations
g.)	Ethical Behaviour of all staff
h.)	Fraud and Fraud Control
i.)	Financial internal controls & segregation of duties
j.)	Financial management, including transactions and reporting
k.)	Governance arrangements (organisational structures, delegations and reporting lines)
l.)	Human resources management & development
m.)	Information technology management
n.)	Media and public relations management
o.)	Occupational health, safety and security
p.)	Performance appraisals and performance management
q.)	Stakeholder relations and management
r.)	Tendering, contracts and procurements

The CEO ensures proper Health Planning and Quality Systems are developed for the province and updated periodically. This includes the following:
a.)	5- year Strategic Health Services Development Plan, 
b.)	5-year Corporate Plan:
c.)	5-year Health Infrastructure Plan
d.)	5-year Health Procurements & Medical Supply Chain Plan
e.)	5-year Health Workforce Plan
f.)	5-year Staff Training & Development 
g.)	Plan
h.)	5-year Information & ICT Networks Plan
i.)	5-year Assets & Equipment Plan that includes: Maintenance Plan and Transport and Logistics Plan
j.)	5-year Emergencies & Disaster Recovery Plan
k.)	5-year District Health Plans (for each individual District)
The CEO requires that all health facilities have developed an Annual Implementation Plan (AIP) which is aligned with both the organisation’s 5-year Strategic Plan and Corporate Plan.

The CEO establishes high-level collaboration relationships to represent Health in the Province. This would include working relationships with;
a.)	Provincial Governor and Governor’s staff
b.)	Provincial Administrator and Administrator’s staff
c.)	Minister for Health and Ministerial staff
d.)	Secretary of Health and staff of NDoH
e.)	District Administrators, DDAs, and District Health staff.

The CEO maintains effective partnership coordination for health services with signing of Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) or Service Level Agreement (SLA) with Christian Health Services and Catholic Health Services, other corporates, NGOs and international Health Partners.

The Board of Governance delegates necessary authority to the Organizations' CEO, Executive Directors, Senior and Middle Managers and other relevant staff, to act in accordance with all legislation, corporate policies, health priorities and delegated authority.
The Board of Governance shall recommend an acting appointment for the Organizations' CEO when required.
The governing body reviews the CEO’s performance at least annually.
The CEO maintains participation of all communities around health facilities within the province.

The CEO ensures that health infrastructure and capital projects are effectively coordinated through a “Projects Unit” to oversee the development, funding and implementation of all Health Infrastructure and Capital Projects.

The CEO ensures a Senior Executive Management Team (SEMT) is appointed to manage the delivery of high-quality health services within the province in accordance with corporate policies relevant to applicable legislation, health policies and health Priorities.
The CEO and SEMT undertake annual review of own performance through 360-degree feedback via a management and staff survey.
The Organisation establishes a Clinical and Public Health Governance Framework to support effective implementation of the National Health Service Standards (NHSS).

The CEO, Director Curative Health Services and the Director Public Health are collectively responsible to ensure all health services and public health programmes are planned, monitored and reported on effectively.

The CEO has an approved “Corporate Risks Management Plan” linked to the 5yr strategic health services development plan, to ensure a framework for the management of risks at all levels of the organisation (i.e.: strategic, programme /projects, and single issues).
There are weekly meetings between Management and staff to discuss work activities planning, AIP implementation, service issues / challenges, safety and quality, etc.
An organisational Health Human Resources (HHR) Unit and Health Workforce Plan is established and functioning effectively every year.
A Health Training Resources Unit (HTRU) and Health Workforce Training Plan is established and functioning effectively within the organisation, every year.
An organisational Assets and Equipment Policy and 5-year Plan is developed, budgeted for, implemented and effectively managed every year.
An organisational Fleet Management Policy, and 5-year Plan is developed, budgeted for, implemented and the transport fleet effectively managed every year.
An organisational Facility Management Program and 5-year Plan is developed, budgeted for, implemented and all maintenance of every health facility effectively managed, each year.

An organisational ICT Services & Network Policy and 5-year Plan is developed, budgeted for, and effectively managed to ensure reliable and consistent support services to all health facilities within the province, each year.
Power, clean water supply and sanitation are made available to all PHA facilities every year.
The organisation’s mission statement and goals are used to direct activities of the health service.
The organisation’s Corporate Plan is produced in consultation with and made known to staff, the community, other relevant health service providers and other stakeholders.
The organisation’s individual health services or hospital departments show evidence of planning and implementation of activities consistent with the Corporate Plan.
The organisation’s Corporate Plan is implemented and revised as necessary. The achievement of the plan is monitored and action taken to address improvements required.
Established lines of responsibility, authority and communication support leadership, teamwork and the organisation through an integration of services.
The organisation structure is reviewed at least every three years or when there is a significant change, such as alteration of the role of the health service or its services.
The organisation’s by-laws and the policies and procedures are consistent with the organisation’s goals, accepted standards, statutory requirements and responsibilities.
Compliance with the organisation policies and procedures occurs throughout the organisational health service.
All organisational policies and procedures are reviewed and revised as necessary.
The Organisation has an approved framework for the development, implementation and ongoing monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of all its health program and projects.
Rights and responsibilities of patients are clearly addressed through policies set by the Board of Governance and there are protocols to deal with matters of complaint.
Respect for patients/clients is evident throughout the healthcare organisation.
The Board of Governance ensures that there is a mechanism for considering ethical issues by an appropriate ethics committee.
Research projects are reviewed, approved and conducted within approved research guidelines by the appropriate ethics committee.

There is compliance with the NHSS at all organisational levels. These include privacy, confidentiality, health records and information management, standards for delivery of health services and compliance with quality standards.

All hospital staff are fully aware and comply to: The Papua New Guinea Medical Board for the registration and discipline of medical practitioners, dental practitioners and allied health workers; and The Papua New Guinea Nursing Council for the registration and discipline of nurses and nurse aides, and for related purposes; when required the PHA Board/CEO reports to the relevant Board to take disciplinary action of a healthcare professional. All Health Workers have approved clinical practice (job scope) based on their competences, performance and professional suitability. There are formal credentialing processes in place that delineates the clinical privileges of medical professionals at the time of appointment/re-appointment and privileges are regularly reviewed with the aid of their peers through the Credentials Committee structure.
Department/Unit Managers/OICs and team ensure all rubbish, flammable materials are safely stored, safely handled and safely practiced.

Newly appointed members of the Board of Governance for the Organization are given a formal orientation. It will include the provision of acts, bylaws and at least a tour of selected health services and introduction to key staff.
Members of the Board of Governance participate in ongoing education to assist them fulfil their role.
The Board of Governance has established their organization's Vision, Mission, Goals, & Objectives to specify and guide the delivery of health services.
The Board of Governance has overall responsibility for the organization's achievements, the quality of healthcare and the organization's resources.

The Board of Governance ensures that there are effective working relations;
•	within all the organisation’s health services
•	with surrounding communities
•	with relevant health care providers
•	with health partners
•	and with other stakeholders
The Board of Governance meets regularly, at least 4 times per year, & makes decisions to ensure arrangements for continuity of governance between meetings.

The Board of Governance has established Committees & Sub-Committees as per their relevance, functions and responsibility in accordance with by-laws, with evidence that such Committees and sub-committees are active.
The members of the Board of Governance and its officers have been duly appointed according to current legislative requirements.

The Board of Governance is held accountable to patients and the community for assuring the delivery of health services that are safe, effective, integrated, high quality and continuously improving through Public Health & Clinical Governance (CG) systems.

CEO & Senior Executive Management team demonstrate leadership to improve clinical care, patient safety and quality of the PHA health systems of care reflected in established Clinical Governance Committees both in clinical and public health settings.
All decisions of the Board of Governance are formally communicated in writing and circulated to staff or individuals of the organization as appropriate.

The Board of Governance periodically reviews its own performance to actively enhance its achievements and to ensure continuous improvement in the quality of care, effective and efficient management of the health services.

The Governing body establishes a policy outlining attendance, functions and roles of executive staff, senior and middle managers, and nominated staff, at the Board of Governance, Committee and Sub-Committee meetings.

There is a flow of information between the Board of Governance, Clinical Governance Committees, Clinical Department Heads, Coordinators of Public Health Programmes, OICs of Wards and District Health Managers, regarding patient safety and quality.
The organisation has an approved 'Code of Conduct' for all healthcare workers which promotes day-day professional conduct and all staff understand its meaning.
There are continuous quality improvement measures demonstrated by management and staff as they continually strive to improve the quality of care.

There is evidence of a 'Critical Incident Monitoring Management' system. This system provides adequate surveillance to recognise major clinical risks and urgent public health events, at the same time, support open disclosure among clinical and public health teams. The serious critical incidents that should be reported are: All deaths in hospital and rural health facilities in PNG especially
Clinical team should conduct Morbidity & Mortality meetings (M&Ms) to review unexpected deaths, particularly those mentioned in Section 3.6.
There is evidence that the SMOs and specialist nursing officers provide adequate clinical supervision within each clinical unit.

Clinicians from multidisciplinary teams should undertake clinical audits through systematic review of patient care against explicit criteria/standards, to identify ways to improve clinical and primary healthcare practice to improve patient outcomes.

There is evidence of national or locally developed 'Clinical Care Guidelines or Standard Treatment Guidelines' that describe the evidence-based care patients should receive for specific clinical conditions and that the patients are aware of the treatment they will receive.

A 'Patient Complaints' mechanism exists as they are a unique source of information for health services on how and why adverse events occur and how to prevent them. Better management of complaints will restore trust and reduce the risk of litigation, through open communication and a commitment to learn from the problem and prevent its recurrence.
The performance of the 'Clinical Public Health Governance Framework' including the CG Advisory Committee and subcommittees are monitored through annual reviews against specified indicators.

The Organisation has initiated leadership and management, at all levels, who are responsible to ensure that all health staff have the required educational qualifications, experience, skills, knowledge and capacities to deliver high-quality and sustainable health care services and support.
The Organisation appoints staff through recruitment, selection and appointment procedures that are consistent with Human Resource policies.

The Organisation has an established health services development plan which outlines clearly the health staffing supply and demand requirements for both clinical and non-clinical health workers, and which is monitored and reported on to the governing Board on a quarterly basis.

There is a 5-year Health Workforce Training Plan to support the 5-year strategic health services development plan, that identifies the required training, upskilling and professional development requirements for both clinical and non-clinical health workers which is monitored and reported to the governing Board on a quarterly basis.

The Organisation has the appropriate “Staffing Skills Mix” needs for both clinical and non-clinical health workers, as determined by application of the Workforce Indicator Staffing Needs (WISN) methodology within the National Health Service Standards (NHSS).
The Organisation ensures that the minimum “Hospital Health Specialist” as determined by the NHSS for Levels of Care and Essential health services.
The Organisation has established a ‘Health Workforce Risk Management Plan’ and process, which identifies, assesses and addresses any risks to health workforce.

The Organisation has a Board of Governance approved policy and procedures covering ‘Occupational Health, Safety and Security (OHS&S) of all health workers within the province, including with health partner organisations/agencies.

The Organisation has established systems to set, monitor and continually improve the performance of the health workforce (clinical and non-clinical) at all levels of the organisation in compliance to General Order.
The Organisation sets policies and systems to strengthen the capacity and productivity of all health workers to improve health care and deliver positive health outcome results.

The Organisation has an established career progression and succession planning system with clear procedures that ensure staff with the requisite skills and capabilities are available in the organisation.

Organisations have a 5-year “Training & Development Plan” approved by the Board covering the whole health workforce (clinical and non-clinical) within the province, including those health workers within health partner organisations.

The Organisation has determined mandatory training accredited by regulatory boards for all health workers as described in the Training Policy for both clinical and non-clinical staff. These include: fire safety, Occupational Health and Safety, hand hygiene, use of protective personal equipment (PPE), environmental cleaning, medication safety for HEOs, Nos and CHWs, cardiopulmonary resuscitation for all health clinicians.

The Organisation has an established and fully equipped “Training and Resource Centre” to support the implementation of the 5- year health workforce training plan, which provides regular training and upskilling courses, and has resources available to assist with ongoing professional development for both clinical and non-clinical health workers.

The Organisation has established a regular process of evaluating the training programmes conducted for all the health workers and reporting to the Board of Governance with recommendations on an annual basis.

The organisation has an established a process for the regular annual review of all clinical and non-clinical training curricula delivered by internal and external providers with a view to ensuring curricula are current and meet existing work environment conditions at all levels.

The organisation maintains effective stakeholder relationships with training and development service providers (e.g., Schools of Nursing & CHWs, Universities, Private Training Providers, NGO Training Providers, etc.) as a means of engaging with collaboration on training programs.

The demand for every item that is stored in a health facility is based on documented past usage data sourced from stock records, and matched where possible with actual and forecast morbidity data for each item.

The supply requisitioning process is done methodically and ensuring that supply meets accurately estimated demand for each item. Supply planning should have;
Stock currently in hand minus any expired stock- in- hand
Duration of stock based on average monthly usage data 
Duration of stock- in- hand and stock- on -order but not received yet.

Storage practices should be consistent with national criteria for storage and store keeping practices.
Storage conditions should meet manufacturers’ requirements to maintain drugs and medical supplies quality. This includes the following aspects of storage management;
Quality of products is affected by high temperature, high humidity, lack of ventilation and exposure to pests and vermin (e.g. rats)
Incorrect labelling 
Expiry dates and products past expiry 
Methodical storage of products in boxes and shelves
Accountability for stock: all receipts and issues are recorded in a stock register and periodic stock- takes carried out to check whether physically available quantities match quantities in stock register. 
There is a designated officer managing the store
Department/Unit Managers/OICs and team comply with the organisation’s ‘No smoking / No Betel-nut policy’ and which is enforced.

Quantities requisitioned periodically should be to meet accurately estimated demand and not to create excess stock of some and under- stocking of others.
The Store should be making sure the stock level does not exceed the Maximum Stock Level and does not fall below the Minimum Stock Level. The following are considered:
Average Monthly Usage
Lead Time 
Minimum Stock Level 
Maximum Stock Level

Avoid the amount of stock that expires in the store prior to being used. Ensure that;
Expired stock is not issued to any patient.
Products that expire first issued first – First to Expire, First Out (FEFO)
Stock that has already expired should not be counted as stock in hand
All expired stock is removed from shelves and disposed in accordance with NDOH’s expired stock disposal procedures.

The Organisation undertakes periodic supply planning in line with the strategic direction identified in the 10-year Master Plan for Medical Supply Chain Management. This would include;
The stock of drugs & medical supplies in its health facilities is provincial stock with stock transferability between health facilities. 
Geographic, seasonal, logistics (road conditions included) and other situations that make stock transfers difficult or impractical noted.
Procuring/requisitioning frequency reduced and,  order quantities increased where logistics difficulties impact on delivery lead times.
A provincial buffer stock of essential items introduced and buffer stock holdings in individual health facilities reduced.

Evidence that the Organisation carries out an Annual Procurement Planning identifying:
The estimated quantity of drugs and medical supply items required for the upcoming year.
The budget required to meet the cost of this estimated need 
Required delivery time frames.
The exercise is carried out by the 31st of October every year and sent to the NDOH Medical Supply Procurement & Distribution Branch (MSPD) during the first week of November every year.

The Organisation undertakes distribution planning, 
management of drugs, medical supplies, vaccines, medical gases and programme stock in accordance with the 10- Year Master Plan for Medical Supply Chain Management. This includes;
The method, time, frequency and cost for transportation to health facilities.
Partnerships for distribution
Transit Stores may be carried out by distribution contractors chosen through a competitive tender process contract.

Ensure that purchase order management is carried out efficiently and that shortcomings in management does not contribute to supply shortages, payment delays to suppliers, and ad hoc emergency procurement.
Ensure there is adherence to agreed terms and conditions with suppliers and there are no negative procurement outcomes due to payment delays to suppliers.

Ensure that the warehouse layout facilitates the efficient and effective movement, with accountable storage of goods that are stored in a warehouse. There should be adequate space for;
incoming goods
a holding area to keep goods until they are stored
an area to store medical gases and cylinders
a cold room for vaccines
refrigerators for items requiring storage in such conditions
a safe and secure area for dangerous and controlled drugs
an area to keep goods that are picked and ready for dispatch
a separate area to keep damaged/expired items until they are disposed according to policy requirements

There should be efficient receiving of goods consistent with terms and conditions in the relevant purchase orders in the warehouse. The goods should be moved to a holding area as soon as possible and to minimise any inconvenience and/or delays to shippers who deliver goods.

Ensure that the picking and packing operation in the warehouse is: 
planned, methodical and efficient
carried out by maximising the labour input
done accurately under supervision 
stock picked and packed are in accordance with the relevant picking slips generated by m-Supply 
all pickings are confirmed in the m-Supply with the least possible delay
The picking schedule should account for at least 80% of items to be picked and packed that week, leaving a maximum of 20% for unscheduled, urgent picking and packing of items that may be required.
The planning and design of health facilities and its refurbishment must be compliant with relevant legislations with safety features ensured.

There is planning and management of internal roads with respect to: 
drop-off and collection of patients/clients
pedestrian safety
ambulance movement
client/consumer/patient transport,
movement of vehicles through the grounds,
speed of vehicles moving through the facility
appropriate parking areas which are safe

The planning and management of walkways within the facility is adequate with respect to;
width
trip hazards
disabled access
movement of clients/consumers 
movement of patient
safety of staff and visitors
All plants and other permanent fixtures are chosen for safety and efficiency and installed and maintained by qualified individuals and as per the manufacturers’ instructions.
The Health Facility has completed the L3-5 Rapid Health Facility Assessment Tool.
There should be clear, well-located internal and external signages to meet the needs of consumers / patients, visitors and staff.
Disability access and facilities meet legislative requirements, which are based on recognised guidelines and is appropriate to the needs of the community and the organisation.

There is a critical incident monitoring system for risks associated with the health facility environment, these risks are investigated, reported and remedial actions taken.
There should be a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for staff, patients, guardians and other visitors to report incidents relating to buildings, roads, walkways, plant, medical devices, equipment, consumables and supplies.
The health facility infrastructure complies with building codes for fire safety.
The local fire brigade performs annual inspections to identify risks.

The fire extinguishers within the facility should fulfil the following criteria:
are in appropriate locations
have a current service tag
have fire hoses
is recorded on the asset registry
is frequently checked
Department/Unit Managers/OICs and staff ensure all fire exits are always kept free of obstruction and fire exit doors open from inside and are not locked from inside.

Department/Unit Managers/OICs and team are trained in the use of fire extinguishing equipment at least annually, in emergency fire response, and understand fire alarm systems / panels around the hospital.

Department/Unit Managers/OICs and team participate annually in mock fire drills. This is reflected in the organisation’s emergency fire plan which details what to do in case of a fire and all staff members have adequate knowledge of the plan.
There should be correct and effective use of equipment via specialty training for staff where required.
There are efficient inventory practices, to ensure the ready availability of supplies and consumables.

The plant and equipment are chosen according to an assessment process that considers:    
compliance with relevant legislation, standards, guidelines and or codes of practice 
intended use and consumer needs
cost benefit
safety 
infection control
energy efficiency and environmental sustainability 
training needs, storage and distribution.
The plant and equipment are being installed, tested and commissioned in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions and by appropriately qualified individuals.

The plant and equipment should receive regular maintenance and cleaning according to a documented schedule with the following requirements:
recording of a log where required
monitored with respect to electrical, thermal radiant and mechanical hazards 
subject to documented processes for procurement, upgrading and replacement

Vehicles are subject to processes for procurement, operation, maintenance and safety that consider: 
government contracts, where relevant
vehicle operators
position descriptions that specify appropriate training and licences 
safe transport of patients
secure transport of health records, medications, equipment or supplies
workplace health and safety issues associated with vehicles, including appropriate seating, access and storage 
reporting of any vehicular accident as an incident.
Medical devices should be used safely with staff involved in the operation of medical devices undergoing necessary training and where necessary, correct licenses have been obtained.
Medical devices are cleaned, sterilised and recommissioned separately from general cleaning processes.
“Supplies and consumables” are generally commodities with a shorter life such as dressings, syringes, disposable gloves, catheters, etc.
The Health Service Organisation can demonstrate preventive maintenance for its equipment so that the plant and the equipment within its Facilities operate safely and efficiently.

Cleaning of equipment should be done according to a documented schedule which describe the frequency of cleaning and the areas / items to be cleaned. It should also describe those areas / items not to be subject to general cleaning (e.g. medical devices).

Plant logs and maintenance processes should ensure that all buildings, including storage areas, plant, equipment, waste management areas and grounds are cleaned, maintained and serviced by qualified persons in accordance with infection control requirements, manufacturer specifications and relevant standards, including maintenance on high-risk plants such as cooling towers and pressure vessels.

The clinical and non-clinical staff can demonstrate handling and management of hazardous material (biological, chemical, radiological, and/or physical), which has the potential to cause harm to humans, animals, or the environment.
There is a radiation safety plan which has a register of all radioactive substances, procedures for the disposal of radioactive waste and radiation equipment.
There is a current asset register maintained by a designated officer.
Security measures are taken to ensure the protection of patients and staff from assault and loss of property; and the Facility from damage and loss.

There is monitoring of water and electricity use, including:
How often is usage monitored? 
How has the organisation improved the efficiency of its energy and water usage?

The Senior Executive Management Team (SEM) of the Health Service Organisation and PHA Finance and Budget Committee members, all Section 32 officers, requisitioning officers and financial delegates, have read and understood the relevant sections of various Acts that are referred to in the Public Finance Manual. These include;
A copy of the PFM Act 1995, PFM (Amendment) Act 2016, PFM (Amendment) Act 2018
Financial Management Manual (2012 and new copy when it is released by Department of Finance)
All Financial Regulations, Instructions and Circulars issued by Central Agencies (but also any that are issued by Provincial Administrations as well),
The Section 32 Officer Learner’s Manual (2014)
The National Procurement Act
The Audit Act 1989
The National Audit Manual
The Public Service Management Act 2014
The General Orders
The CEO and Board of Governance ensure compliance with Central Ministry instructions to implement effective PFM and its accountability requirements to national and provincial governments.
There is a credible budget planning process where budget and revenue estimates align to organisational resource needs and strategic service plans.
There is a credible budget implementation process across the organisation.
The Health Care Organisation has internal budget controls in place to ensure the accountable usage of public funds to the organisation.

The Health Care Organisation have strong working relationships with Central Ministries to improve alignment of approved budget estimates with service delivery plans and disbursement of cash with implementation requirements.
The Health Care Organisation has strong working relationships with Provincial and District Administrations to improve provincial resourcing of primary and rural health care.

The Health Service Organisation has established a fully functional Finance and Budget Committee to ensure that the formulation, oversight and reporting on the organisation’s budget is conducted in a proactive way and is compliant with national requirements.

The Health Service Organisation has established a fully functional Project Steering Committee (PSC), established to direct and oversee both planning and the development of health infrastructure across the organisation.
The Health Service Organisation has established a fully functional Audit & Risk Management Committee established to make effective use of the internal audit function.

Public Finance Management accountability requirements of the CEO and Board of Governance are fully understood and followed, to ensure the efficient and transparent usage of public and other resources to improve health outcomes in the province.
The CEOs must know their mandated role as the Chief Accountable Officer and the PFM powers that they command, who they are responsible to report to on overall PFM and performance reporting, in what format, how often to report and what to do with the reports in terms of strategic decision making before the Board.
The CEOs must also know their role in enforcing accountability requirements across all other officers working in the PHA in meeting mandatory performance objectives of the PHA and ensuring the effective management of its day-to-day operations.
The Health Service Organisation reviews quarterly financial performance and financial statements for the Board of Governance.
The Board of Governance approves budget estimates and annual financial statements.
The Health Service Organisation has an annual budget timeline developed, an internal budget process and annual budget cycle requirements.
The Health Service Organisation Fee structure has been established and gazetted to keep track of the revenues that it generates, such as hospital user fees and other medical charges.
Provincial and district consultations are conducted after the budget is passed by Parliament and approved by Provincial Assemblies

The Health Service Organisation maintains an operating account. There should be effective usage and maintenance of this account.
There is an internal operating account manual with the following criteria;
No one individual 
oversees identifying a spending need
is ensuring it is in line with the organisation’s plan for the year and delivers value for money (i.e. proper procurement guidelines have been followed).
does verification of both budget appropriation and funds which are available through warrant authority and CFCs.
making a commitment.
reviewing the commitment to ensure it is in line with financial procedural requirements
administering the transaction
carrying out a review of the transaction

The Health Service Organisation maintains a Health Services Improvement Project (HSIP) trust account. The HSIP staff must effectively manage the trust account by adhering to;
The HSIP Trust Instrument
The Trust Account Manual of procedures
The Public Finances Management Act (PFMA)
The DPM General Orders, and
Any memorandum of understanding between the Development Partners and the Government of PNG.
Bank reconciliations are conducted weekly to ensure that the Health Service Organisations’ underlying financial records are accurate and reliable.

Budget adjustment requests are tracked and reported.
There should be summaries of requisition requests and Section 32 approvals that require the redistribution of cash funds or actual budget adjustments in IFMS/ the accounting system used by the organisation.
There should be Board approved guidelines that specify the conditions under which budget adjustments within and across expenditure votes can take place and these guidelines are circulated to;
Section 32 officers
Financial Delegates
Commitment Clerks
Authorizing Officers and Certifying Officers, Directors of Public and Curative Health
the heads of the Church and Catholic Health Services District health managers and other budget holders
Annual reports should be prepared for publication to meet PFM Act, PHA Act and Audit Act requirements
Basic accounting qualifications are required for accounts and audit officers.

The Public Financial Management Manual for the Health Service Organisation is read and used as a guideline and tool for best practice.
Relevant sections of the PFM Manual should be read, utilised and referred to in the daily operations of the organisation by the following officers;
The CEO
The Director of the Corporate and Support Services (CSS)
The Finance Manager
All Financial Delegates
Accountants and clerks
All planning officers
Budget officers
Members of various finance and budget committees.
District Health Managers
Training and support are provided by Central Agencies and NDoH throughout the year.
Training and capacity building work delivered through donor partner programmes.

The Organisation has developed and implemented a “5-year Information and Communications Technology (ICT) Plan” which is aligned with the Organisation’s Strategic Development  Plan, to ensure relevant infrastructure (hardware, software, networks, systems, etc) are enabled in all health facilities, to fully support health services delivery operations and delivery of key health program & project outcomes.

The Organisation has implemented appropriate policies and procedures for the keeping, accessing, storage, archiving and disposal of records and their security, in line with all relevant legislations, regulations and by-laws.
Every patient has a medical record which is sufficiently detailed to enable continuity of care, education and research and to facilitate clinical coding.
Information is made available to staff in a user-friendly format to assist with patient care and management of services.

The Organisation has embedded effective and transparent governance, which prioritises ICT investment, ensures decisions consider outcomes across health, manages risk, enables clinical leadership and provides accountability. Medico-legal requirements for information are met.

The Organisation has adopted a policy to fund the implementation of a common hospital patient electronic health record system across all provincial hospitals linked to a National Master Index (ICD 10) or the e-National Health Information System (e-NHIS).

Develop strategy to encourage and support the implementing of non-urgent telehealth outpatient care service to achieve both expenditure savings and service efficiencies because of reduced travel and associated costs for patients.
There is a need to stabilise existing ICT infrastructure, implement ICT systems at new L5 health facilities, consolidate duplicate systems and build the foundations for the future.
Improve information management, including secure sharing of patient information to improve patient safety, quality of care and care coordination.
Build organisational capacity, capability and credibility to deliver and use ICT systems.

The Health Care Organisation, their partners and the communities engage in planning to meet the health needs of a geographic catchment for a defined population.
This planning should be integrated through vertical alignment (through levels of care) and horizontal alignment (through the integration of public health and clinical services) and is consistent with NHSS levels of care and delineated roles. 
The following are taken into consideration:
Changing population characteristics and population needs.
Emerging clinical evidence and technologies 
Projection of future needs influenced by changes in populations, disease patterns and treatment technologies.

Public health planning relating to planning for a public health issue (or issues) for a specific population cohort and targeting a particular geographical catchment. This should consider:
Communities are involved in planning for desired services closer to where people live
A focus on health promotion, health protection and prevention
Increase focus on planning for emerging priorities and pandemics, and immunisation
Routine integrated outreach services to “hard to reach” areas
Integrated school health programs
All health facilities have access to clean water and improved sanitation
 Programmes to reduce stunting in communities.

There is ongoing planning for a specific service -streams (e.g. medicine, surgical, O&G, paediatrics cardiac, renal) to provide evidence based, safe, high quality and appropriate clinical services. This type of planning targets a population or geographical catchment as part of planning for the clinical service. The planning should consider;
Key service areas which include prevention, promotion and protection, primary health care, ambulatory care, clinical - acute care, specialised care and mental health.
A standard set of capability requirements for most acute, specialised and sub specialised services in line with NHSS.
Encourages clinical risk management. 
Articulates credentialing, privileging, qualification and training requirements for staff.
Identifies the relationships and interdependencies between health services across the Organisation and other facilities.

The health needs in the Clinical Services Plan are reflected through the life course (birth to death) with continuity of care between public, private and other healthcare providers for the following:
Well population who live independent lives
At risk population with a probability of developing a health condition or an adverse health outcome
Easy identification and intervention of ill health and who, without intervention, may progress to acute or chronic consequences
Acute consequences and conditions who require treatment.
Chronic conditions that are long-lasting and/or leave a residual disability
End of life care with fatal conditions and those who are dying.
The Health Service Organisation has adequate Healthcare Project Management services that impacts any projects that work to improve a healthcare-related function.
The Board of Governance ensures there is a functioning Partnership Committee.
The Partnerships Committee is chaired by an appointed member of the Board of Governance.
The Partnerships Committee is meeting regularly.
Reports from the Partnerships Committee are submitted to the Board of Governance with recommendations.
The Partnership Committee has equal representation of women.

During supervisory visit, Supervisors follow nine (9)    Supervisory Steps, i.e.;
Observations of Department / Clinical Unit (physical environment)
Full Staff (Team) Meeting
Review all the evidence / data: i.e.: Registers, NHIS tablet, ANC cards, medical records, critical incident reports.
Discuss within the team, relevant Elements and Components, fill out an initial score.
Conduct “Brainstorming” with the full team to summarise agreed actions and recommendations to be taken for each component within each relevant element.
Complete each Element Summary, scores, and calculate percentages; Each element summary provides a total score /% as well the summary of agreed actions & recommendations.
Complete onsite in-service training: based on identified topics or priority topics from the staff (team) meeting.
Complete the 'Supervision Performance Scorecard & Summary Report' (front sheet summary) and distribute copies to Hospital Dept/Division/Unit Heads/Clinical Directors/Public Health Unit/OICs and other relevant officers.
Provide Feedback and plan for the next supervisory visit.
